messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Sex: Sex, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leilani is a 19-year-old fisherman who works on her uncle’s boat out of a small coastal town. She has been with her boyfriend, Kai, for just over a year. What brought her to the clinic was a quiet desperation—she was afraid she was becoming someone she did not recognize.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago, on a warm evening at the marina. Leilani had just finished cleaning the catch and was walking along the dock toward her bicycle, which she used to ride home every day. She heard footsteps behind her—quick, heavy—and before she could turn, she saw a man on a bicycle speeding past her toward a young woman who was kneeling by the water, untangling a net. The man stopped, shouted something Leilani couldn’t make out, and then struck the woman with something—a pipe, Leilani later thought—and pushed her into the water. The woman screamed, there was a splash, and then silence. Leilani froze, her body locked in place, unable to move or call out. She did not run toward the woman. She did not shout for help until it was too late. By the time anyone came, the woman had drowned.

That moment has not let her go. The memory forces its way into her mind without warning—sometimes triggered by the creak of a bicycle wheel, the sound of hurried footsteps, or any sudden splash. But just as often the memory comes without any image at all: Leilani will be standing on the deck of the boat, and suddenly her chest will tighten, her hands will shake, and she will be flooded with a wave of guilt so intense she wants to vomit. She cannot see the woman’s face in those moments, only feels the shame of her own inaction. She has come to believe that she should have protected that woman, and that she failed—a failure that, in her mind, defines her now.

Leilani has learned to avoid the conditions that might bring the memory on. She no longer rides a bicycle; she walks or gets rides. She avoids the marina at the end of the day, and she flinches every time she hears footsteps behind her. At home, she spends hours on her phone, scrolling through videos or playing games, anything to keep her mind from drifting to that dock. She works as many shifts as her uncle will give her—sometimes twelve hours on the water, coming home exhausted—because when she is alone with her thoughts, the guilt rises and she cannot bear it. Her body, she has come to feel, is no longer on her side. It reacts before she has even registered danger: her heart pounds, her muscles tense, she feels ready to fight or flee, even when she is sitting safely in her living room. She has trouble concentrating on simple tasks. When something takes longer than expected—a boat repair, a delivery—she immediately assumes something terrible is happening.

The avoidance has seeped into her relationship. She has stopped having sex with Kai, not because she does not love him, but because the idea of being so vulnerable, of letting go of control, terrifies her. She is afraid of her own anger. She has never hit anyone, but she feels a rage building inside her—toward the man who killed the woman, toward herself for doing nothing—and she is terrified that one day she will lose control and do something terrible. So she keeps a tight lid on everything. She pushes Kai away when he tries to comfort her, worried she will snap.

What finally brought Leilani to therapy was a fight with Kai, in which he told her she was a different person now, cold and distant, and that he did not know how to reach her. She realized she was losing the one person she trusted. She came in hoping to find a way back to herself, but what she is most afraid of is that the guilt will never fade, and that the woman’s drowning will always be her fault.
